Module 1 · Business Planning

What is my business, who is it for and what problem does it solve?

Lesson 1 of 5Approximately 20 minutesSelf-paced

Create one plain-English sentence that defines your business as it stands today—and use it to guide your next decisions.

01
Your output

One working definition of your business covering what you sell, who it is for, the problem or goal, and the practical result.

02

The 60-second answer

A definition is a decision tool

Your business definition tells you which enquiries to take, which products to make and which requests are a distraction.

A usable definition has four parts: what someone buys, who buys it, their problem or goal, and the practical result.

An accurate, slightly clumsy definition is more useful than a polished, vague one.

Work it through

1Write it for yourself first

This is for decisions such as: do I take this booking, make this product or say yes to this collaboration? Marketing wording comes later.

2Separate the four parts

Pull apart what you sell, who it is for, the problem or goal, and the practical result. If the last two are missing, you have described the work rather than its purpose.

3Use words that carry information

Replace words such as “quality”, “bespoke”, “supportive”, “modern”, “affordable” and “tailored” with the fact underneath them.

4Test a real decision

Make the sentence specific enough to guide something you are weighing up this month. If it settles nothing, it is still too broad.

5Treat it as version one

Date it. Changing the definition later means the business is being run on evidence—not that you got it wrong.

What this looks like in practice

Before: “I’m a dog groomer who really cares about animals.”

“I groom dogs at the owner’s home for people with nervous or elderly dogs within a 20-minute drive of [town], who find a salon visit stressful or impractical, so the dog is washed, clipped and comfortable without leaving the drive.”

This immediately helps her decide whether to accept bookings 45 minutes away.

Before: “I make gluten-free bakes.”

“I bake gluten-free bread and rolls for independent cafés and farm shops in [county] that want a coeliac-safe option they can list on the menu, so they can serve customers they currently turn away.”

A market stall would be a different customer and problem—a deliberate decision rather than drift.

Before: “I do admin support, tailored to each client.”

“I handle inbox, diary and supplier admin each month for small charities with no office staff, so the person running the charity is not doing admin at nine o’clock at night.”

A one-off database project for a large company clearly sits outside the definition.

03

Activity 1

Think it through

Answer from what has actually happened. If you have not traded yet, answer from what you intend and add (A) beside assumptions.

04

Activity 2

Build your definition

Place the useful facts from Activity 1 into these four parts. Your sentence will build underneath as you type.

My definition · version 1

I provide what for who, who problem, so result.

Vague-word check

Check whether your sentence relies on words that could describe almost any business.

05

Activity 3

Test a real decision

Does your definition make the decision clearer?

Ask yourself

  1. Could someone correctly say what I sell and who buys it?
  2. Does anything in my current work sit outside this definition, and is that deliberate?
  3. Which part am I least sure about, and what evidence would tell me the answer?
06

Use AI carefully

Use it to test clarity—not choose your direction

Write the sentence yourself first. AI does not know your customers, skills, capacity or market.

Find the vague words

Ask AI to identify vague wording, missing parts and unevidenced claims without rewriting your sentence.

Test reader understanding

Ask what a reader thinks you sell, who buys it and what problem it solves—then where they had to guess.

07

The one thing to remember

A definition is only doing its job when it can rule something out.

If your sentence lets you say yes to every enquiry, product idea and opportunity, it is a description rather than a definition.

What if I sell more than one thing, or to two types of customer?

Write a separate definition for each, then compare them. If they share a customer or problem, you may have one business with two offers. If they share nothing except you, that may mean twice the marketing effort for the same income.

I have not sold anything yet. Can I still do this?

Yes. Write from what you intend to sell and who you believe needs it, then mark the assumptions. Those become the first things to test.

Do I need to choose a niche first?

No. Define what is true today. Narrowing comes later, once you have evidence about who buys and who does not.

Is this the sentence I put on my website?

Not yet. This version is for you. Customer-facing wording is separate work covered in Module 4: Brand and Messaging.

Your next step

Give it a genuine first-read test

Read your definition aloud to someone who does not know your business. Ask them what you sell and who buys it. Change anything they get wrong.
